chapter_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream (Values and Dispositions)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 5 periods = 225 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 45min

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Reading the Letter — Fact, Opinion and Core Ideas

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.82): paired discussion — communication timeline and social media.
Let us discuss (p.85-86): identify facts vs. opinions in selected statements.

time_bands.activity: Open with the before-reading activity at p.82: students arrange means of communication (carrier pigeons to mobile phones) on a quick timeline drawn on the board, then share one reason the means they prefer. This activates prior knowledge and sets the context for Kurien's preference for letters.

Teacher reads Kurien's letter aloud from p.82–85 while students follow in their textbooks; pause at natural breaks to let the narrative settle. Emphasis on tone — a grandfather writing to a grandson across time — helps students hear the register before any formal questioning begins.

Work through the fact-or-opinion task at p.85–86: teacher reads each of the eight statements aloud, students decide individually, then share with the class and justify. Guide the class to notice how Kurien's personal judgements ('I knew I could make a more meaningful contribution') differ structurally from factual claims about events.

periods.teacher_notes: Kurien's letter mixes personal reflection with historical fact — students often mistake confident first-person assertions for facts; help them trace the distinction through verb choices and hedging language. The before-reading communication timeline also surfaces naturally into the letter's opening contrast between telephone and written correspondence, so let those threads connect. Students who finish the fact/opinion task early may begin annotating Kurien's stated values in the margin.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for timeline

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis — Integrity, Partnership and Legacy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.86-87): extract questions on letter-writing and fast-paced world.
Let us think and reflect Part II (p.88): questions on Padma Vibhushan and Kurien's values.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.87): read Extract 2 and answer questions on grandmother's role.

time_bands.activity: Work through Extract 1 questions at p.86–87: the fill-in-the-blank on the 'fast-paced world', the assertion-reason MCQ on letter-writing, and the true/false on Kurien's view of letters as a class apart. Students respond individually, then a class discussion confirms and deepens each answer.

Move to the Part II questions at p.88: class discusses why Kurien wrote to Siddharth, what his decision to work in Anand reveals about his values, and what his remark that 'failure is not about not succeeding' means for young readers. Encourage students to support answers with specific phrases from the letter.

Brief discussion: 'Life is a privilege, and to waste it would be wrong.' Students share one-sentence opinions; teacher draws out Kurien's message about selfless service and its long-term impact on society. Homework task at p.87 (Extract 2 — grandmother's role) is explained and assigned.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the fact/opinion work done with the letter's statements, this unit pushes into inference — students must now explain why Kurien made the choices he did, not just what he did. The Padma Vibhushan anecdote at p.88 is a strong anchor: Siddharth's challenge to 'earn your own reward' is both personal and universal and rewards close reading. Flag Extract 2 (p.87) on the grandmother's role as self-study for students who want deeper engagement.

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Evelyn Glennie — Listening and Stress-Pattern Speaking

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.93): listen to Evelyn Glennie passage and match vocabulary words.
Let us listen (p.93): true/false statements and short comprehension responses.
Let us speak (p.94): read aloud noun/verb pairs with correct syllable stress.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Evelyn Glennie briefly — a percussionist who became deaf as a child yet rose to world-class mastery. Ask students to predict: how might someone without full hearing still experience music?

Teacher reads the Evelyn Glennie transcript (p.100) aloud at a measured pace while students listen with books closed. Students then complete the matching task at p.93 (percussionist, impaired, vibrations, determination, gradual). Check answers together.

Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students complete the true/false statements at p.93, then answer the three short-response questions ('How did Evelyn turn her disability into strength?'). Pairs compare before whole-class discussion.

Shift to speaking: teacher models syllable stress on 'present' (PREsent / preSENT), then students read the five noun/verb pairs at p.94 (PROduce/proDUCE, CONtract/conTRACT, etc.) aloud in turns. Teacher corrects stress placement with the whole class listening.

periods.teacher_notes: Evelyn Glennie's story connects thematically to Kurien's message about perseverance — both figures refused to let circumstance define their contribution. For the listening tasks, read the transcript at natural speech speed so students practise real-time comprehension rather than dictation pace. The syllable-stress exercise at p.94 is brief but precise: insist students mark stress before reading aloud so the distinction between noun and verb forms becomes kinaesthetic.

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Pause and Chunk Aloud — Then Write a Gratitude Letter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.95): read 'Don't Quit' with pause markings; chunk second stanza.
Let us write (p.95-96): draft a personal letter to grandparents with two required elements.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains pausing and chunking as tools for the listener, modelling short (/) and long (//) pauses on two lines of 'Don't Quit' (p.95). Students then read the first set of stanzas aloud with the printed pause markings, followed by individual attempts to chunk the second stanza ('Life is queer with its twists and turns…') and read it back to the class.

Transition to writing: briefly review the conventions of a personal letter (salutation, body paragraphs, closing). Display the two required elements from p.95-96 on the board — how the grandparents' actions inspired you, and how that inspires your own contribution to society.

Students draft their letter independently. Teacher circulates, prompting those who struggle by asking: 'What specific lesson did they teach you — a story, an act, a habit?' Encourage students to include at least one concrete example before moving to the second paragraph about contributing to society.

Two or three volunteers read their letters aloud; class offers one strength and one suggestion for each. Students revise one sentence of their choice before submitting. The complete draft — including any revision — is finalised within this sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking and writing tasks share a common thread: both ask students to shape their voice for a specific audience, whether oral or written. In the chunking exercise, watch for students who mark pauses mechanically without reading for meaning — redirect them by asking what the speaker wants the listener to feel at each pause. For the letter, remind students that Kurien's letter itself is a model: he names specific events (Padma Vibhushan ceremony, the choice to stay in Anand) rather than speaking in generalities.

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Language in Context and India's Agricultural Revolutions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.88): replace underlined words with correct synonyms from box.
Let us learn (p.89): match expressions from the text with their meanings.
Let us learn (p.90-91): fill in blanks choosing between contractions and possessives.
Let us explore (p.96): group research and sharing on White, Green, Blue Revolutions.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.90): insert em dash or en dash correctly in eight sentences.

time_bands.activity: Synonyms task at p.88: teacher reads each sentence aloud; students choose the correct word (essential, swift, lifelong, momentary, useful, splendid) to replace the underlined word. Discuss why each synonym fits — linking meaning back to Kurien's letter.

Matching task at p.89: students work with the six expressions from the text (in all humility, hold their heads high, to be quite honest, etc.) and match each to its meaning in Column 2. Verify as a class and practise using two of the expressions in original sentences.

Contractions vs. possessives task at p.90–91: teacher highlights the distinction between its/it's and your/you're using two examples from the board, then students fill in all six blanks. Quick whole-class check; explain the em dash/en dash task (p.90) as homework.

Groups of four use the textbook passage at p.96 on the White, Green, and Blue Revolutions as a launch pad. Each group decides one angle to explore (who, what impact, what region), prepares a spoken two-minute summary, and one representative shares with the class. Teacher connects Kurien's White Revolution to the cooperative model described in the letter.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary tasks at p.88–89 are deliberately drawn from the letter itself — students who worked closely with Kurien's language in earlier units will find the synonyms and expressions familiar, making accuracy more likely. For the contractions/possessives task, the common error is treating 'its' as a contraction; a quick mnemonic ('no apostrophe, no shortcut') can anchor the rule. The beyond-text group task should not exceed its allotted time — a focused two-minute share is more productive than an open-ended discussion that cannot conclude within the sitting.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student distinguishes between fact and opinion and draws inferences about a writer's values using an informational letter as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Kurien's letter to grandson Siddharth: nation-building, integrity, Padma Vibhushan, failure as effort.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements from Dr. Kurien's letter and identify each as a Fact or an Opinion by writing F or O in the blank.
1. Dr. Kurien started his working life soon after India became independent.
2. Writing letters is a class apart from other kinds of writing.
3. Dr. Kurien received the Padma Vibhushan in 1999.
4. Most comparisons we make are illusions of perfection.

options.text: Dr. Kurien started his working life soon after India became independent.
Writing letters is a class apart from other kinds of writing.
Dr. Kurien received the Padma Vibhushan in 1999.
Most comparisons we make are illusions of perfection.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. F — This is a verifiable historical claim about when Kurien began working.
2. O — This is Kurien's personal judgement about the value of letter-writing, not a verifiable fact.
3. F — The year 1999 and the award are confirmed details in the letter.
4. O — This is Kurien's philosophical assertion about human comparison, not a factual claim.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student distinguishes between fact and opinion and draws inferences about a writer's values using an informational letter as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Kurien's letter to grandson Siddharth: nation-building, integrity, Padma Vibhushan, failure as effort.
items.item_stem: Dr. Kurien tells Siddharth that failure is not about not succeeding but about not putting in one's best effort. What does this reveal about the values Kurien considers most important, and how does his own life story — choosing Anand over a career abroad — support this belief? Write your response in three to four sentences.

expected_elements: Identifies integrity and honest effort as Kurien's core values.
Links his choice to stay in Anand despite other opportunities.
Connects his definition of failure to personal responsibility, not outcome.
Uses at least one specific detail from the letter.

items.item_stem: After listening to the passage about Evelyn Glennie, match each word from the passage in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Word (Column A)|Meaning (Column B)
percussionist|slow and steady over time
impaired|a person who plays drums and similar instruments
vibrations|the ability to keep going despite difficulties
determination|damaged or weakened
gradual|physical sensations caused by sound

answer_key.right: a person who plays drums and similar instruments
the ability to keep going despite difficulties

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student comprehends a spoken passage and retrieves specific details and vocabulary meanings using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Evelyn Glennie's gradual hearing loss, Ron Forbes's tuning exercise, sensing music through the body.
items.item_stem: Ron Forbes told Evelyn Glennie, 'Don't listen through your ears — try to sense it some other way.' What did Evelyn discover as a result of following this advice, and what does her discovery tell us about how human beings can adapt to overcome a challenge? Write your answer in two to three sentences.

expected_elements: States that Evelyn learned to sense notes through different body parts.
Names specific detail: higher drum felt from waist up, lower from waist down.
Draws an inference about human adaptability or determination.
Response is grounded in the passage, not general knowledge.

items.item_stem: Read each of the following word pairs aloud. For each pair, say which form is the noun and which is the verb, and demonstrate the difference in syllable stress clearly. Word pairs: PROtest / proTEST; REcord / reCORD; PERmit / perMIT.

expected_elements: Correctly identifies noun form (stress on first syllable) for each pair.
Correctly identifies verb form (stress on second syllable) for each pair.
Pronounces stress difference audibly, not just by naming it.
Maintains steady pace without hesitation between pairs.

items.source_lo: Student applies stress, pause, and chunking techniques to read aloud with clarity and expression using oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Syllable stress on noun/verb pairs; pause markings on poem 'Don't Quit' stanzas.
items.item_stem:
Read the following lines from the poem 'Don't Quit' aloud. Mark where you would place a short pause (/) and a long pause (//) to help a listener follow the meaning. Then read the lines with your markings, explaining in one sentence why you chose the longest pause where you did.

Lines: 'When things go wrong as they sometimes will / And the road you're trudging seems all uphill / When the funds are low and the debts are high / And you want to smile but you have to sigh'

expected_elements: Places short pauses at natural phrase boundaries within lines.
Places a long pause at the end of a complete thought or stanza break.
Reads with audible difference between short and long pauses.
Gives a reason that connects pause placement to meaning for the listener.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student composes a purposeful personal letter with specific supporting detail using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Letter to grandparents: lessons inherited, values shaped, contribution to society inspired.
items.item_stem: Write a short informal letter (about 80 words) to a grandparent or an elder you admire, thanking them for one specific lesson — a habit, a story, or an act of kindness — that they shared with you. Use a proper salutation, at least two body sentences with a specific example, and a warm closing.

expected_elements: Uses correct informal letter format: salutation, body, closing.
Names one specific lesson, habit, or act — not a general statement.
Explains what the lesson taught the writer in concrete terms.
Maintains warm, personal tone appropriate for the recipient.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student composes a purposeful personal letter with specific supporting detail using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Letter to grandparents: lessons inherited, values shaped, contribution to society inspired.
items.item_stem: Dr. Kurien ended his letter by urging Siddharth's generation to work tirelessly for the larger good of the country and humanity. Imagine you are Siddharth, now grown up, writing a letter to a younger child in your neighbourhood who feels that one person cannot make a difference. Write a letter of about 120 words in which you share what you learned from your grandfather's life and why you believe individual effort matters. You may draw on any idea from Dr. Kurien's letter.

expected_elements: Adopts Siddharth's perspective convincingly throughout the letter.
References at least one specific idea from Kurien's letter (e.g., integrity, Anand choice, failure as effort).
Addresses the child's doubt directly and offers a reasoned counter-view.
Uses appropriate letter format and an encouraging, personal tone.

items.source_lo: Student applies vocabulary in context and distinguishes between contractions and possessives using language from the section as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Synonyms (magnificent, fleeting, instant, core, valuable, abiding); expressions (in all humility, hold their heads high); its/it's, your/you're distinctions.
items.item_stem:
Choose the correct word from the brackets to complete each sentence below.
(i) The cooperative movement had _______ (its / it's) roots in the village of Anand.
(ii) Dr. Kurien believed that _______ (your / you're) character is tested when you choose duty over comfort.
(iii) The ceremony was truly _______ (its / it's) own reward — dignified and deeply moving.
(iv) The dairy workers felt _______ (their / they're) contribution was finally being recognised.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) its — possessive, referring to the movement's roots. (ii) your — possessive, referring to the reader's character. (iii) its — possessive, referring to the ceremony itself. (iv) their — possessive, referring to the workers' contribution.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student applies vocabulary in context and distinguishes between contractions and possessives using language from the section as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Synonyms (magnificent, fleeting, instant, core, valuable, abiding); expressions (in all humility, hold their heads high); its/it's, your/you're distinctions.
items.item_stem:
The expressions below are taken from the world of Dr. Kurien's letter. Write one original sentence for each expression that shows you understand its meaning. Use a context connected to school, community, or daily life — not a copy of any example from the textbook.
(a) in all humility
(b) to the best of your ability

expected_elements: Each sentence places the expression in a fresh, plausible context.
Sentence (a) conveys modest acknowledgement without self-deprecation.
Sentence (b) conveys wholehearted effort applied to a specific task.
Neither sentence reproduces textbook phrasing or Kurien's letter directly.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student researches and presents findings on real-world social initiatives using project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: White Revolution (Kurien), Green Revolution (Swaminathan), Blue Revolution (Chaudhuri); cooperative impact on India.
items.item_stem: The White Revolution led by Dr. Verghese Kurien transformed India into the world's largest milk producer through the cooperative model. In a group of three or four, prepare a two-minute spoken presentation that explains: (1) what problem the White Revolution solved, (2) how the cooperative structure made it possible, and (3) one way its impact is still felt today. Each group member must speak for at least one section of the presentation.

expected_elements: Accurately names the milk shortage or farmer exploitation as the problem addressed.
Explains cooperative ownership: farmers as producers and shareholders.
Cites a contemporary impact (Amul, milk availability, rural income).
All group members contribute; presentation is within the time limit.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student researches and presents findings on real-world social initiatives using project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: White Revolution (Kurien), Green Revolution (Swaminathan), Blue Revolution (Chaudhuri); cooperative impact on India.
items.item_stem: India's three major agricultural revolutions — White (dairy), Green (food grains), and Blue (fisheries) — each addressed a different national need. Create a one-page comparison chart with three columns (one per revolution). For each revolution, fill in: the leader's name, the sector it changed, one key method used, and one lasting result. Below the chart, write two sentences explaining which revolution you think had the broadest benefit for ordinary rural families, and why.

expected_elements: Chart correctly names Kurien (White), Swaminathan (Green), Chaudhuri (Blue).
Each column includes sector, a method, and a result — all factually grounded.
Opinion statement names one revolution and provides a reasoned justification.
Justification references rural or community benefit, not just production figures.
